approved: Broadband, Communications and the Digital Economy

Introduced the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill, allowing successful bidders in the April 2013 auction of 126 megahertz of digital dividend spectrum to begin services early by limiting datacasting regulation, ahead of the spectrum being cleared of broadcasting services by 31 December 2014.

Criticised the government for giving the House committee only three working days to examine the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill 2013, noted the Police Federation of Australia's concern for 56,000 police officers' access to emergency services spectrum, and recounted the communications minister's boast at a New York conference that bidders would end up wearing 'red underpants' on their heads.

Argued that wireless audio device users occupy the spectrum being sold as if it were vacant, noting five years of unresolved dialogue between the Australian Wireless Audio Group and the government over roughly 120,000 of an estimated 150,000 units at risk, cited about 100 such devices used at a recent Eurovision Song Contest venue, and foreshadowed a coalition amendment requiring the minister to certify adequate alternative spectrum before auctioned bands are released early.

Argued the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill 2013 is sensible as far as it goes but fails to fix deeper problems with the spectrum auction, citing research showing an average international reserve price of 80c per megahertz per head of population against the government's $1.36, and noted the maximum spectrum a single bidder could acquire had been raised from 20 to 25 megahertz.

Argued the government's $1.36 per megahertz per head of population reserve price for the digital dividend spectrum auction is too high, estimated it would cost about $1.5 billion to acquire enough spectrum to cover 22.6 million people, and backed the Police Federation of Australia's call for 20 megahertz to be set aside for public safety communications.

Criticised the government for failing to develop a transition plan for the estimated 120,000 wireless audio devices operating in the digital dividend spectrum, noted a major Australian reality television show can use up to 60 such devices at once, and said the Australian Wireless Audio Group has made at least nine submissions to government or ACMA over the past seven years without resolution.

Explained the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill 2013 to constituents as a technical measure letting successful digital dividend spectrum auction bidders begin services before the restack of broadcasting spectrum is completed, expected by 31 December 2014, and warned that failing to pass the bill this sitting would undermine bidder certainty in the April 2013 auction.

Explained the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill 2013 to a lay audience using the shift from AM to FM to digital radio as an analogy, and noted the government had provided the community broadcasting sector with an additional $12.5 million and digital community radio with $13.5 million, each over four years, plus $2.2 million in annual ongoing funding.

Closed debate on the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill 2013, explaining a safeguard included to prevent circumvention of the datacasting rules, thanked the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Infrastructure and Communications and the shadow minister for communications for cooperating on an amendment, and commended the bill to the House.

The Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Dividend) Bill 2013 was introduced to allow early telecommunications services in the 126 MHz digital dividend spectrum, with auction in April 2013 and spectrum clearance by 31 December 2014, and to limit datacasting regulation to commercial and national broadcasters. The Insurance Contracts Amendment Bill 2013 was introduced to improve the insurance market by removing impediments to electronic communication, making the duty of disclosure easier, and clarifying rights and obligations.
